newsitem.title: USA: More low-fat foods rolling out, thanks to ingredients.
newsitem.headline: More low-fat foods rolling out, thanks to ingredients.

text.p: The food industry is cooking up more low- and no-fat offerings for consumers, thanks to a growing list of ingredients that promise higher-quality, better-tasting products.
"When you take fat out of a food, it's a complicated endeavor," explained Eric Allen, a spokesman for the Calorie Council, which tracks reduced-fat foods.
To make up for the texture, flavor, moisture and other positive attributes of fat, food companies must use ingredients such as modified fats, corn starch and gums.
"Manufacturers have gotten better and better at it (making low-fat foods)," Allen added.

The food industry continues to increase its introductions of low- and no-fat foods, with 2,076 new offerings in 1996, up from 1,914 in 1995, according to Lynn Dornblaser, publisher of New Product News.

Total food product introductions, however, fell last year to 13,266 in 1996 from 16,823, a decline of more than 21 percent. Dornblaser said 1996 marked the first decline in new food introductions of that magnitude since the 1970s.
As a result of the overall decline, reduced-fat introductions accounted for 15.6 percent of all new foods in 1996, up from 11.4 percent in 1995.

Dornblaser added that reduced fat foods are growing in acceptance due to improvements in the quality and flavor of these products. "Fat-free sour cream," she said, "is very close to being indistinguishable from full-fat sour cream."

"They (food companies) see growth in the 'light' segments of all these different categories," Mike Klacik, vice president of marketing for Cultor Food Science North America, said Monday. "The thing they're looking for is the best possible taste they can deliver."

Cultor, a unit of Cultor Oy of Finland, in 1996 formally launched a reduced-calorie fat known as salatrim, which goes by the brand name Benefat. Salatrim, which is made from soybean oil, has only five calories per gram, instead of nine calories per gram for traditional fat.
Benefat was first introduced in Hershey Foods Corp.'s reduced fat baking chips, Klacik said.

Another food ingredient company, Opta Food Ingredients Inc., makes corn starch-based ingredients for reduced-fat foods, including its patented OptaGrade. OptaGrade, a texturizing agent,is used in products like low- and no-fat sour cream and a no-fat butter substitute spread.
The Massachusetts-based company also mades a natural cellulose product that adds moisture to lower-fat baked goods, Lewis Paine, chairman of Opta Food, Paine said.
"Our job is to service the (food company or fast-food restaurant) customer so that the consumer is happy," Paine said.
While Cultor and Opta said their products are naturally derived and have no side effects, the reduced-fat food arena has seen some criticism over fat substitutes.

Procter & Gamble Co.'s food additive olestra has been criticized by a consumer watchdog group for allegedly causing gastrointestinal problems for some consumers. Procter & Gamble has defended olestra, which is used in snacks, saying that most consumers will not have any complications.

Overall, consumers are eating more reduced-fat products. The Calorie Council's latest consumer survey showed 88 percent of adult Americans used reduced-fat products on a regular basis in 1996, up from 73 percent in 1993.
For example, Nabisco Holdings Corp.'s Snackwells line of low- and no-fat snacks and baked goods now has about 70 different products on the grocery shelves, compared with a six-item line in 1992.
"The whole platform is based on new technology in the food processing side of things," Ann Smith, director of marketing communications for Nabisco, said.
